title: Management & Leadership
tagline: Learn to run teams and organizations — from first-time supervisor to executive leadership.
summary: Management is the craft of getting results through other people: setting direction, delegating, coaching, budgeting, and leading change. This roadmap covers the people skills and operational disciplines that turn strong individual contributors into credible managers and executives.

detail.description: Managers plan, organize, lead, and control work through other people. The classic POLC framework (planning, organizing, leading, controlling) still describes the job well.
detail.why: Management is a career change, not a promotion — the skills barely overlap with individual contributor work, and starting deliberately beats being thrown in.
learn: Read O*NET task statements for general and operations managers
Explain the four POLC functions with your own examples
Identify 3 managers you've had and what made them good or bad
Decide whether you want to manage people or processes (both are real careers)
tasks: Plan, direct, or coordinate the operations of public or private sector organizations, overseeing multiple departments or locations.

detail.description: The recurring work of management: setting goals, structuring work, directing and developing people, and measuring results — a weekly cycle, not a checklist.
detail.why: Most new-manager failures come from skipping one function (usually measuring or organizing). Seeing the whole loop keeps you balanced.
learn: Write one SMART goal for a team function
Draft a simple weekly operating rhythm (1:1s, reviews, planning)
Explain the difference between accountability and responsibility
Audit your week: how much time goes to each function?

detail.description: Managers need working literacy in how the business makes money: revenue models, unit economics, budgets, and the basic financial statements.
detail.why: You cannot defend a budget or a hire without understanding the numbers behind them.
learn: Read a simple P&L and explain each line
Calculate gross margin and contribution margin for a product
Understand fixed vs variable costs and operating leverage
Follow the Accounting & Finance roadmap basics if numbers feel weak

resources.title: Khan Academy — Finance and capital markets

detail.description: Management communication is mostly structured listening and clear writing: briefs, one-pagers, expectations, and difficult conversations delivered with respect.
detail.why: Most management failures are communication failures — unclear expectations, absent feedback, or silence during change.
learn: Write a one-page team brief anyone could act on
Practice delivering corrective feedback using the SBI model
Run a meeting that ends with owners and dates
Practice active listening in your next three conversations

detail.description: Building a team means hiring deliberately (structured interviews, honest scorecards) and delegating with clear outcomes, authority levels, and follow-up — not abdication.
detail.why: Your output as a manager is the team's output. Delegation is how you multiply; hiring is how you compound.
learn: Write a delegation brief: outcome, authority level, check-in cadence
Build a structured interview guide for one role
Practice the delegation levels (do it / do and report / decide and inform)
Identify one task you should have delegated last quarter

detail.description: Great managers coach: regular 1:1s that belong to the employee, feedback that is specific and timely, and development plans that stretch people without breaking them.
detail.why: People leave managers more than companies. Coaching quality drives retention, engagement, and performance simultaneously.
learn: Run employee-owned 1:1s for a month (they bring the agenda)
Deliver five pieces of specific, behavior-based feedback
Write a development plan with one stretch assignment
Practice asking before telling (coaching questions)

detail.description: Meetings are where management happens or gets wasted: clear purpose, right people, documented decisions, and follow-through. Decision hygiene (who decides, how) matters more than tools.
detail.why: Teams inherit their meeting culture from their manager. Clean meetings compound; chaotic ones bleed the calendar.
learn: Write a decision doc: context, options, recommendation, owner
Try a no-agenda-no-meeting rule for two weeks
Practice disagree-and-commit in a real decision
Audit one recurring meeting for elimination

detail.description: Sustainable motivation comes from purpose, autonomy, mastery, and fairness — not just bonuses. Managers shape all four through how work is assigned and recognized.
detail.why: Engagement follows the manager, not the perks. Understanding intrinsic motivation changes how you assign and recognize work.
learn: Map each team member's motivation drivers in 1:1s
Redesign one task to increase autonomy
Recognize effort publicly and correct privately
Explain expectancy theory (effort → performance → outcome) simply

detail.description: Workplace conflict is inevitable; unmanaged conflict is optional. Managers surface disagreements early, mediate fairly, and separate people problems from structural problems.
detail.why: Avoided conflict grows until it costs you your best people. Early, fair mediation is a core management muscle.
learn: Identify the 5 conflict-handling styles and when each fits
Mediate a practice dispute: hear both sides, reframe to interests
Separate task conflict (healthy) from relationship conflict (corrosive)
Write a team working-agreement to prevent repeat conflicts

detail.description: Operational planning translates strategy into a sequenced plan: objectives, owners, milestones, dependencies, and review cadence — quarterly with weekly checkpoints.
detail.why: Teams drift without a plan everyone can recite. The manager owns the clarity, not necessarily the content.
learn: Run a quarterly planning session producing one page of committed goals
Break a goal into milestones with owners and dates
Build a dependency map for a 6-week initiative
Review progress weekly and re-plan without drama

detail.description: Managers build and defend budgets: headcount plans, operating expenses, and the trade-off conversations that decide what gets funded.
detail.why: Budget fluency is the entry ticket to senior management — the person who understands the numbers gets the seat.
learn: Build a department budget template (people, tools, programs)
Variance-explain a month: why did you overspend or underspend?
Practice a budget-defense narrative tied to business outcomes
Understand capex vs opex at a high level

resources.title: Khan Academy — Finance and capital markets

detail.description: Improving how the work gets done: mapping processes, finding bottlenecks, standardizing, and measuring — using lean thinking rather than big frameworks.
detail.why: Managers who improve the system outperform those who push people harder inside a broken one.
learn: Map one team process end-to-end and time each step
Find the bottleneck and design one experiment to relieve it
Write a standard-work doc for a recurring task
Measure before/after and report honestly

detail.description: Managers combine data with judgment: define the question, gather minimal sufficient evidence, decide, and review the outcome. Avoiding both gut-only and analysis-paralysis traps.
detail.why: Leaders who show their reasoning build trust — and teams that can repeat the process without you.
learn: Write a one-way vs two-way door decision classification
Run a simple A/B or before/after read on one team change
Keep a decision journal for a quarter and review it
Define the metric that would change your mind

detail.description: Managers sponsor projects others run: clear charters, resourcing, unblocking, and milestone reviews — delegating the mechanics to project management professionals.
detail.why: Understanding the PM discipline makes you a better sponsor and a better candidate for operational leadership roles.
learn: Read the Project Management roadmap basics
Write a one-page project charter for a real initiative
Practice a 15-minute milestone review agenda
Learn when to re-scope instead of re-pressure

detail.description: Strategy is choosing where to play and how to win: understanding customers, competition, and capabilities, then committing resources accordingly.
detail.why: Even front-line managers translate strategy into daily choices — understanding the logic prevents locally-rational, globally-wrong decisions.
learn: Summarize your organization's strategy in three sentences
Run a simple SWOT for your team's function
Explain trade-offs: what will you explicitly NOT do?
Read one classic strategy framework (Five Forces or similar)

detail.description: Designing how work is organized: team boundaries, roles, spans and layers, and decision rights — so structure follows strategy rather than history.
detail.why: Structure determines communication paths and career growth. Managers redesign pieces of the org constantly, formally or not.
learn: Audit your team's structure for unclear ownership
Define decision rights for three recurring decisions
Compare functional vs pod structures for your context
Draft a reorg proposal with risks and mitigations

detail.description: Leading change means sequencing communication, involving affected people early, expecting resistance as information, and measuring adoption — not announcing and hoping.
detail.why: Most initiatives die at adoption. Managers are the multiplier between a plan and a changed organization.
learn: Stakeholder-map a change by influence and impact
Draft a communication plan with audiences and messages
Interview three resisters — treat objections as data
Define and track one adoption metric

detail.description: Situational leadership: directive with novices, coaching with learners, supporting with competent performers, delegating with experts — matching style to person and stakes.
detail.why: One-style managers cap their teams. Flexibility is the differentiator between managing tasks and developing people.
learn: Classify each direct report's competence and commitment per task
Practice switching styles deliberately for a month
Ask your team which style helps them most
Identify your default style and its blind spots

detail.description: Communicating upward and outward: crisp status (headline first), bad news early with options, and presentations built around decisions rather than information dumps.
detail.why: Careers are made or lost in how leadership experiences your clarity under pressure.
learn: Rewrite a status update: headline, impact, ask
Prepare a 5-slide decision deck (situation, options, recommendation)
Deliver bad news within 24 hours with a recovery plan
Practice the 30-second version of every big topic

detail.description: The second-line shift: you develop managers rather than people, align direction across teams, and build the operating system (reviews, planning, talent processes) they run inside.
detail.why: This is the real jump to senior leadership — your impact compounds through other leaders' consistency.
learn: Coach a manager on their 1:1 practice, not their tasks
Run a manager sync focused on shared standards
Review skip-level signals without undermining managers
Build a simple talent review for your org

detail.description: The management ladder runs supervisor → manager → senior manager/director → VP → C-suite, in every industry. Parallel tracks (program leadership, general management) and pivots (consulting, entrepreneurship) abound.
detail.why: Management careers are built on scope and results, not tenure — knowing which scope you want shapes every job choice.
learn: Map the ladder in your industry with typical scope per rung
Decide people-leadership vs operational-leadership emphasis
Identify the two experiences missing from your profile
Set a five-year target and the role that bridges to it

detail.description: Paths into management: promotion from strong IC performance, team-lead roles, management trainee programs, and small-business leadership — plus the transition mistakes to avoid (doing, not delegating).
detail.why: The first 90 days set your trajectory. Getting deliberate about the transition — before or just after the title — prevents the classic failure modes.
learn: Volunteer to lead one project with 2-3 contributors
Write your own 30/60/90 plan for a first management role
List your top five 'do it myself' triggers and delegation plans
Find a manager mentor before you need one

detail.description: Management credentials are optional but useful: Lean Six Sigma belts (ASQ) for process-heavy roles, project credentials for delivery roles, and the MBA for broad general-management and executive tracks.
detail.why: Credentials rarely make the manager — but they signal seriousness, structure your learning, and open HR screens in larger organizations.
learn: Compare Lean Six Sigma Green/Black Belt vs an MBA for your track
Check job postings in your target industry for credential asks
Consider a leadership course cohort for the network, not the certificate
Budget realistically — degrees are major investments

certs.name: Lean Six Sigma Green Belt
certs.note: Exam-based credential in process improvement method (DMAIC); useful for operations-heavy management.

detail.description: Managing your own boss: understanding their goals and pressures, bringing solutions not surprises, and negotiating priorities openly when capacity is finite.
detail.why: Every manager is also managed. Doing it well earns autonomy, resources, and advocates for your next role.
learn: Write your boss's top three goals and pressures
Practice the no-surprises rule on your next status
Prepare options with a recommendation, not open questions
Negotiate one priority trade-off explicitly this month
